# Connection pooling with PgBouncer

Postgres gives every client connection its own server process, and once `max_connections` is
reached it refuses new clients with `FATAL: sorry, too many clients already`. PgBouncer sits between
the clients and the server. Clients connect to it as if it were the database, and it lends each of
them a real server connection from a small pool. In the lab's tests, with PgBouncer 1.25 in
transaction mode and a pool of 10, this let far more clients connect than Postgres allows, but it did
not make a single connection any faster to open.

## Connection cost

Most of the time it takes to open a connection goes into checking the password. PgBouncer checks it
too, so opening a connection through PgBouncer takes about as long as opening one directly. Starting
the Postgres process itself takes about a millisecond.

With 80 clients connecting at once, PgBouncer was slower than a direct connection. It runs on a
single thread and checks the passwords one at a time, while 80 Postgres processes check theirs in
parallel. A pooler saves more time when connecting is slow for other reasons, such as TLS over a
network.

## Clients beyond max_connections

With `max_connections = 100`, two hundred clients connecting directly at once got roughly a hundred
connections and a hundred refusals. Through PgBouncer all 200 connected, and Postgres ran at most 10
processes for them. In transaction mode a client holds a server connection only while its
transaction is open, and between transactions it costs PgBouncer a few kilobytes instead of a
Postgres process.

## Pool size and queueing

Clients that cannot get a server connection wait in PgBouncer until one is free. Fifty clients that
each need 100 ms of database time finish in about 100 ms when they connect directly, and in about
500 ms (50 / 10 × 100 ms) through a pool of 10. The pool keeps Postgres down to 10 busy processes
during a burst, at the cost of that wait, so `default_pool_size` is best set to the number of queries
Postgres can run at once, which is roughly its number of cores.

## Transaction pooling and session state

In transaction mode, the server connection behind a client can change from one transaction to the
next. Anything that lives on the connection itself therefore becomes unreliable:

- `SET`, which no longer sticks (`SET LOCAL` inside the transaction works)
- temporary tables, which can vanish or linger for the next client
- `LISTEN`, session advisory locks and `WITH HOLD` cursors
- prepared statements, unless PgBouncer 1.21 or later tracks them with `max_prepared_statements`

The [PgBouncer notebook](../notebooks/pgbouncer_playground.ipynb) shows the temporary-table case with
thirty clients that each create a table in one transaction and read it in the next. Under load, the
second transaction often lands on a server connection that never saw the table.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Drivers behind PgBouncer

psycopg 3 prepares a statement once it has run five times and asyncpg prepares every statement, so
both need PgBouncer 1.21 or later with `max_prepared_statements` above 0. On an older PgBouncer,
preparation has to be turned off (`prepare_threshold=None` in psycopg, `statement_cache_size=0` in
asyncpg).
:::

## When to use PgBouncer

| situation | PgBouncer? |
|---|---|
| serverless or short-lived processes connecting per request | yes |
| many app instances, each with its own pool | yes, it caps the server side |
| hundreds of idle connections (dashboards, queue workers) | yes |
| protecting Postgres from bursts | yes, as a limiter |
| one monolith with a well-sized SQLAlchemy pool | little; it already reuses connections |
